concepts.name: Types of Food Chains: Grazing vs. Detritus Food Chain
key_dimensions: Structural difference: starting point (living plant vs. dead organic matter)
Relative energy contribution: detritus chain dominates energy flow in most ecosystems
UPSC trap: which chain is more dominant in forest/aquatic ecosystems and why
Interconnection between the two chains via detritivores and decomposers

concepts.name: Trophic Levels: Definition, Numbering, and Limits
key_dimensions: Why food chains are typically limited to 4–5 trophic levels (10% energy law)
Assignment of trophic level to omnivores — fractional trophic levels concept
UPSC trap: producers are trophic level 1, not 0; distinction from decomposers
Top carnivores vs. apex predators: overlap and distinction in trophic positioning

concepts.name: 10% Law of Energy Transfer (Lindeman's Law)
key_dimensions: Origin: Raymond Lindeman (1942) and its basis in thermodynamic laws
Implication for food chain length and pyramid of energy
Why eating lower on the food chain is ecologically efficient (policy angle)
UPSC trap: 10% is an approximation — actual transfer ranges from 5–20% depending on ecosystem

concepts.name: Food Web: Structure, Complexity, and Ecosystem Stability
key_dimensions: Food web as interconnected food chains — how it increases ecosystem resilience
Relationship between biodiversity and food web complexity
UPSC trap: more complex food web = more stable ecosystem (keystone species removal destabilizes it)
Difference between food web and ecological network; trophic cascade as a consequence

concepts.name: Ecological Pyramids: Energy, Biomass, and Number
key_dimensions: Which pyramids can be inverted and under what ecosystem conditions
Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright — a frequent UPSC assertion question
Inverted biomass pyramid in aquatic ecosystems (phytoplankton vs. zooplankton)
Inverted number pyramid example: single tree supporting many insects and birds

concepts.name: Producers (Autotrophs): Role and Diversity in Food Chains
key_dimensions: Photoautotrophs vs. chemoautotrophs — chemoautotrophs as base of deep-sea food chains
UPSC trap: chemosynthetic bacteria at hydrothermal vents bypass solar energy — exception to solar-based food chain rule
Net Primary Productivity (NPP) as the actual energy available to next trophic level
Role of phytoplankton as primary producers in marine ecosystems (50% of global NPP)

concepts.name: Decomposers and Detritivores: Role in Food Chain vs. Food Web
key_dimensions: Distinction: detritivores (earthworms, millipedes) physically break down vs. decomposers (fungi, bacteria) chemically break down
UPSC trap: decomposers are NOT typically shown in food chains but are critical to nutrient cycling
Their role in connecting grazing and detritus food chains
Saprotrophic nutrition and its ecological significance in closing biogeochemical cycles

concepts.name: Keystone Species and Their Disproportionate Role in Food Webs
key_dimensions: Definition: species whose impact is disproportionate to their biomass/abundance
Classic example: Sea otters → sea urchins → kelp forests (trophic cascade)
Indian context: Tigers as keystone species — Project Tiger's ecological rationale
UPSC trap: keystone species ≠ dominant species; confusion between umbrella, flagship, and keystone species

concepts.name: Trophic Cascade: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up Control
key_dimensions: Top-down control: predator regulates prey population (e.g., wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone)
Bottom-up control: primary productivity determines upper trophic level biomass
Real-world application: overfishing of top predators causing jellyfish blooms
UPSC angle: trophic cascade as justification for large carnivore conservation policy

concepts.name: Biomagnification and Bioaccumulation in Food Chains
key_dimensions: Distinction: bioaccumulation (within one organism over time) vs. biomagnification (across trophic levels)
Classic pollutants: DDT, methylmercury, PCBs — fat-soluble, non-biodegradable
UPSC trap: biomagnification increases WITH trophic level — top predators (including humans) most affected
Policy link: Stockholm Convention on POPs, ban on DDT, and food safety implications

concepts.name: Omnivores and Their Ambiguous Position in Food Chains/Webs
key_dimensions: Why omnivores complicate linear food chain models — occupy multiple trophic levels simultaneously
Concept of mean trophic level and fractional positioning
UPSC trap: humans as omnivores — their trophic level is approximately 2.2, not 2 or 3
Ecological implication: omnivory increases food web stability by providing dietary flexibility

concepts.name: Parasitic Food Chain: Structure and Ecological Significance
key_dimensions: Direction of energy flow: large host → smaller parasite → even smaller hyperparasite
UPSC trap: unique among food chains — pyramid of number is always inverted in parasitic chains
Role of parasites in regulating population sizes and maintaining biodiversity
Examples: Oak tree → gall wasp → parasitoid wasp → hyperparasite

concepts.name: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) vs. Net Primary Productivity (NPP)
key_dimensions: GPP = total photosynthesis; NPP = GPP minus plant respiration — what's actually available to herbivores
Ecosystem comparison: tropical rainforests have highest NPP; open oceans have low NPP per unit area but high total
UPSC trap: high biomass ≠ high NPP (e.g., old-growth forests have lower NPP than young growing forests)
NPP as the foundational metric for assessing food chain carrying capacity

concepts.name: Secondary and Tertiary Consumers: Carnivore Classification and Overlap
key_dimensions: Strict carnivores vs. facultative carnivores and their placement in food webs
UPSC trap: a species can be a secondary consumer in one food chain and tertiary in another within the same food web
Apex predators: no natural predators — their removal causes mesopredator release
Indian examples: Tiger (apex), Leopard (mesopredator), implications of tiger decline

concepts.name: Energy Flow: Unidirectional vs. Cycling of Matter
key_dimensions: Fundamental principle: energy flows unidirectionally (cannot be recycled) while matter/nutrients cycle
UPSC trap: unlike nutrients, energy cannot be recycled through an ecosystem — lost as heat at each level
Second Law of Thermodynamics as the ecological basis for energy loss
Policy implication: why ecosystems need a continuous external energy input (sunlight)

concepts.name: Mutualistic and Symbiotic Interactions as Non-Linear Food Web Connections
key_dimensions: How mutualism (e.g., mycorrhizae, nitrogen-fixing bacteria) supports primary productivity and base of food chain
UPSC trap: mutualistic relationships are not part of the food chain per se but critically influence its structure
Pollinator networks as a food web adjacent concept — collapse affects herbivore layer
Distinction between food web (energy/feeding) and interaction web (all ecological interactions)

concepts.name: Aquatic Food Chains: Marine vs. Freshwater Specific Features
key_dimensions: Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Small fish → Large fish → Marine mammals: classic marine chain
UPSC trap: inverted biomass pyramid in open ocean — phytoplankton (low standing biomass, high turnover) supporting large zooplankton biomass
Freshwater food chains: role of periphyton and macrophytes as producers vs. marine phytoplankton
Dead zones and hypoxia: how eutrophication disrupts aquatic food chains

concepts.name: Food Chain Length: Determinants and Ecological Theories
key_dimensions: Two main hypotheses: energetic constraint hypothesis vs. dynamic stability hypothesis
UPSC angle: longer food chains in more productive and stable ecosystems
Effect of habitat size and species richness on food chain length
UPSC trap: food chain length is NOT solely determined by energy — body size, foraging efficiency also matter

concepts.name: Indicator Species and Food Chain Integrity as Environmental Health Metrics
key_dimensions: Concept of bioindicators: species whose presence/absence signals ecosystem health (e.g., lichens for air quality, otters for water quality)
Relationship between food chain integrity and ecosystem services
UPSC angle: IUCN Red List categories and their link to trophic level vulnerability (top predators more extinction-prone)
Policy connection: EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) using trophic analysis to assess project impacts

concepts.name: Human Interventions Disrupting Food Chains: Invasive Species, Pollution, and Overexploitation
key_dimensions: Invasive species as food web disruptors — Nile perch in Lake Victoria eliminating 200+ cichlid species
Overfishing and fishing down the food web — shifting baseline syndrome
UPSC trap: introduction of exotic species can either add a new trophic level or collapse existing ones
Indian context: water hyacinth, Lantana camara disrupting terrestrial food chains; legal framework under Biological Diversity Act
